transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-14 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Dr. Lena Ortiz (CTO - Cascade Analytics), Markus Heine (Head of IT), Priya Sengupta (Compliance Manager), Evan Roos (Data Engineer)
Shared links: Redwood airgap checklist (link), pilot SOW template (link), preliminary pricing matrix (link)

Summary:
Cascade is evaluating a fully physically isolated, on-prem deployment of Redwood Private in their regulated analytics facility. Primary concerns: offline update process, hardware compatibility (older racks, mixed NVIDIA cards), key management and HSM integration, audit logs/retention, and procurement timeline. They want clear pilot success criteria and an offline patching/workflow model (signed artifacts, checksums) that meets their compliance team.

Topics covered:
- High level architecture options: Private (air-gapped) vs Dedicated vs hybrid fallback
- Offline update model: signed bundles, USB/hot-swap approval, checksum verification and SDLC
- Hardware compatibility: GPU models on site (V100, T4, some A30), driver/kernel constraints, container runtime
- Security/compliance: KMS/HSM integration, SSO, RBAC, audit log retention, SOC2 evidence
- Ops/process: patch windows, rollback, telemetry (what can be sent out), and physical handoff procedures

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): All right hi everyone, thanks for carving time today. quick intro, I'm Maya, AE for this account, and Daniel here is our solutions engineer, he'll dive deep on the on-prem bits.
[00:12] Dr. Lena Ortiz (CTO): Hi thanks Maya, appreciate it. we just want to make sure we cover compliance gating and the hardware checklist early.
[00:18] Markus Heine (Head of IT): yeah, I'm just coming off of an audit so.. happy to walk through inventory.
[00:23] Daniel (Redwood SE): great, quick agenda — we'll run architecture options, deep dive into the air-gap update flow, and then hw compat and questions. sound good?
[00:30] Evan Roos (Data Eng): yep, perfect.
[00:32] Maya: cool, first question for scope — are you considering any hybrid fallback to hosted for emergencies, or must it be totally tethered?
[00:41] Priya (Compliance): for regulated pipelines, we need the inference to be fully local. No egress of raw telemetry or model artifacts. limited metadata logs are ok but must be encrypted and retained on-prem.
[00:52] Daniel: understood. Redwood's private option supports a fully air-gapped deployment; our control plane can be completely customer-hosted or we can provide signed update bundles that you physically transfer.
[01:05] Dr. Lena: Can you explain the signed bundle approach? how do we validate authenticity without network checks?
[01:12] Daniel: Sure. The common pattern is we produce a signed tarball — essentially a release package signed with our private key — and you verify the signature with our public cert before installing. The package includes a manifest with checksums for every artifact. There's an offline verification tool we provide that runs a local signature check and checksum verification.
[01:30] Markus: is the verification tooling allowed to run on an air-gapped machine? we have strict rules about executables.
[01:36] Daniel: Yes, the verifier is a single static binary, FOSS-licensed-ish, and we can provide source. It can be run inside your secure environment; no outbound calls. we also support vendor-signed bundles if you prefer to re-sign after internal review.
[01:50] Priya: how do you handle keys? we use an HSM for all signing operations and key material can never leave the HSM.
[01:58] Daniel: We have two patterns: 1) Redwood signs releases and you validate; 2) we deliver unsigned artifacts that you sign internally with your HSM. For the former, if you insist keys never leave, you'd choose option 2 and re-sign. We also support integrating with common HSMs for in-place key operations.
[02:16] Dr. Lena: ok that helps. next — hardware. We have a mix: a few racks with V100s, several T4s, and two newer nodes with A30s. Drivers are RHEL8 base, kernel is 4.18, and we have some older compilers.
[02:33] Daniel: good to know — A30s are fine, V100s will work but performance will be lower; some of our optimized kernels expect newer CUDA versions. We can ship quantized model variants to fit memory constraints. What's your target latency and throughput?
[02:48] Evan: for batch jobs we do 10–20 rps, but for the clinician-facing UI we need p95 latency < 600ms for a 512-token request.
[02:57] Daniel: 600ms p95 on a V100 might be tight depending on model size. If you go for a 7B quantized profile it's doable with careful batching; for 13B models you should plan for A30/A100 class hardware.
[03:14] Markus: are you able to run multiple model variants on the same node to save capacity? we'd prefer consolidation.
[03:18] Daniel: yes, we support co-located model variants with resource isolation, but you'll need to reserve GPU memory and use container isolation. There's a small overhead; we can provide suggested node sizing per variant.
[03:30] Speaker 2 (transcription glitch): um, there's also the KV cache, the K-A cache, I mean KV cache warming and persistence — how's that handled in an airgap?
[03:40] Daniel: good call — kv cache persists in local storage and is kept behind the customer's file system. For true air-gapped installs we don't ship cache to Redwood; persistence is local and we support snapshot export/import via signed packages if you want to pre-warm.
[03:54] Priya: audit logs — what do they contain? are we able to scrub PII before anything is written?
[03:59] Daniel: logs are configurable. By default we capture request metadata (route, model id, token counts, duration) and redaction hooks let you drop or hash user text. Full request bodies can be turned off. Retention windows are configurable; we can ship logs to your SIEM locally.
[04:15] Dr. Lena: what about SSO and RBAC? We use SAML with Okta.
[04:20] Maya: Redwood supports SAML SSO for the management plane; for private deployments you can run our auth service locally and connect to Okta over your internal IdP. RBAC maps to LDAP groups too.
[04:32] Markus: kernel/CUDA compat — our ops team is sensitive to upgrading kernels. will Redwood images require kernel bumps?
[04:38] Daniel: We try to support a range. For older kernels we provide fallback container runtimes with older libcuda drivers, but some optimizations (new attention kernels) require newer CUDA. We'll give a compatibility matrix and specific driver min versions.
[04:52] Evan: about updates — do you support hot patching or do we need scheduled maintenance windows?
[04:57] Daniel: updates are installed during maintenance windows. The typical offline flow is: 1) Redwood releases signed bundle; 2) your ops team imports and validates; 3) deploy to canary node(s) in isolated env; 4) run smoke tests; 5) promote. We can script rollback to previous bundle via manifest.
[05:15] Priya: can we audit the build pipeline? we'd like to see SBOMs and build logs for model artifacts.
[05:21] Daniel: yes, we produce SBOMs for the runtime and model packaging, and we can include reproducible build metadata. For highly regulated customers we can also allow an independent build in your environment.
[05:33] Maya: timeline question — what's a realistic pilot?
[05:36] Dr. Lena: the procurement window is usually 8–12 weeks, but we want technical validation first.
[05:41] Maya: typically a 6–8 week pilot covers HW validation, deploy of a 7B quantized model, and an eval with your clinical prompts.
[05:49] Markus: do you have references for sites with similar air-gapped setups?
[05:52] Maya: yes, we can share two anonymized case studies — one in pharma and one in med-imaging — both had physical transfer workflows and HSM integration. I'll include them.
[06:02] Evan: on telemetry: what minimal telemetry does Redwood require to operate?
[06:06] Daniel: none required. The platform can run with zero outbound telemetry. For performance tuning we optionally collect aggregate token counts and latency but only if preapproved; everything can be blocked or kept internal.
[06:18] Speaker 3 (background): mm-hmm
[06:20] Dr. Lena: procurement/contract concerns — do you offer a perpetual offline license or is it subscription?
[06:27] Maya: for private on-prem we typically do an annual subscription with an option for multi-year commitments; there are add-ons for extended support, on-site assistance and enhanced retention. We can also structure a license fee that is capitalized depending on procurement rules — we'll surface both models in the SOW.
[06:42] Priya: what about vulnerability patching windows? we have to apply CVE patches within 30 days for critical severity.
[06:49] Daniel: we support a signed emergency patch channel. If a critical CVE appears we'll prepare a hotfix bundle and coordinate a verified install. We'll also provide mitigations if immediate patching is not feasible.
[07:02] Evan: curious about model sizes and disk footprint for local model store. how big is a 7B quantized package?
[07:08] Daniel: typically 7B quantized ~ 6–8GB; 13B quantized ~ 12–16GB. We recommend at least 1.5x model size for working space and logs per model. We'll put exact numbers in the HW spreadsheet.
[07:20] Markus: what's the CPU footprint for concurrency? we don't have infinite CPU.
[07:23] Daniel: depends on batching. For small batch sizes CPU overhead is modest; we give per-model recommended vCPU and threading configs. For high concurrency we advise separate CPU-only inference proxies with batching handled on the GPU nodes.
[07:36] Dr. Lena: if we want to pre-warm the kv cache with clinical prompts, can we import a cache snapshot?
[07:41] Daniel: yes, snapshot import is supported. We'll provide tooling to export/import signed cache snapshots; again, all signed and checksummed.
[07:52] Maya: quick commercial question — do you have a sense of the rough delta between Dedicated reserved nodes versus Private air-gapped in terms of price?
[07:59] Daniel: variable, but Private is higher because of on-prem support, packaging, and one-off engineering for air-gap. The delta can be ~20–40% depending on level of onsite support and HSM integration. We'll provide precise tiers in the pricing doc.
[08:15] Priya: one more on compliance — do you provide audit artifacts for auditor sign-off?
[08:20] Maya: yes, we'll produce deployment attestation packages, SBOMs, configuration manifests, and our SOC2 -- those will be in the security pack.
[08:28] Markus: last ops item — what's your recommended process for emergency rollbacks if a bundle causes a regression?
[08:33] Daniel: the manifest includes a previous bundle pointer; we keep a local cached copy of the previous release. Rollback is automated through the installer and should be scriptable to a single command during maintenance windows. We recommend canarying first.
[08:48] Dr. Lena: ok this is helpful. next steps?
[08:51] Maya: I'll send the airgap checklist, the security pack, and two anonymized references. Daniel will assemble a hardware compatibility spreadsheet and a proposed pilot plan. Can we aim to reconvene after Markus shares the server inventory?
[09:03] Markus: yes, I can share inventory by next Friday.
[09:07] Priya: procurement will need the SOW and pricing; we'll aim to review internally the week after.
[09:12] Maya: cool, we will target those dates. thanks everyone.
[09:16] Dr. Lena: thanks, talk soon.

(End of recording — rough transcription; occasional speaker labels may be mismatched.)
